strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap: jointly generating 3D molecular coordinates while maintaining an explicit synthesis-aware reaction graph, rather than treating synthesizability as a post hoc score.
The proposed SYNSPACE dataset is a useful contribution, pairing building-block reaction graphs with multiple low-energy conformers at a scale that enables training such models.

The method is technically plausible and reasonably well specified, combining masked discrete diffusion for building-block/reaction graphs with continuous coordinate flow matching and chemistry-aware constraints.

Empirical results are broad: de novo generation is compared against several recent 3D molecular generators, with metrics for validity, retrosynthetic solve rate, energies, PoseBusters validity, FCD, diversity, and novelty.
Ablations identify important contributors, especially chemistry-aware constraints and self-conditioning, and the inpainting/linking experiments demonstrate an interesting zero-shot use case.
weaknesses: The main claims of state-of-the-art 3D molecule generation are somewhat overstated because SYNCOGEN operates in a much narrower, curated building-block/reaction space than atom-level baselines; many metrics are not fully apples-to-apples.
The synthetic-accessibility advantage is partly built into the representation and constraints, so it is hard to disentangle learned generative quality from procedural reaction-grammar enforcement.

SYNSPACE is limited to 93 building blocks and 19 simplified reaction templates, with important chemistry omissions such as protecting groups, stoichiometry, directing effects, stereochemical granularity, and macrocycles; this limits generality to realistic medicinal chemistry.
Reproducibility appears incomplete from the manuscript text: dataset and code availability placeholders are blank, and key implementation details may not be sufficient without released resources.
Retrosynthesis evaluation is performed on only 100 generated samples for some metrics, which weakens confidence in the synthesizability comparisons.

The conditional/inpainting evaluation is small, using only three protein-ligand cases, and relies on docking and AlphaFold3-style qualitative checks rather than stronger prospective or experimental validation.
The method intentionally breaks some equivariance through the dummy-atom/visibility scheme and positional embeddings; the consequences are acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

Some results temper the strongest claims: for given reaction graphs, SYNCOGEN is slightly worse than RDKit ETKDG on conformer coverage/matching, and several geometry distribution metrics in the appendix are not uniformly best among baselines.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: connecting 3D molecular generation with explicit synthesis-aware reaction graphs, which is a relevant gap between conformer generation and practical molecule design.

The proposed representation over building blocks, reactions, reaction centers, and coordinates is reasonably well motivated, and the paper gives useful implementation detail for the joint masked discrete diffusion and continuous flow setup.
The new SYNSPACE dataset, if released with code and generation scripts, could be useful as a controlled benchmark for studying synthesis-aware 3D generation.

The paper includes several baseline comparisons, ablations, and chemically motivated metrics beyond simple RDKit validity, including retrosynthesis solve rates, PoseBusters checks, and force-field/semiempirical energy proxies.
weaknesses: The main empirical claims are substantially overextended. The reported gains largely follow from constraining generation to a tiny procedurally generated space of 93 building blocks and 19 reaction templates, so high validity and retrosynthesis scores do not convincingly demonstrate broad synthesizable molecule generation.

The baseline comparison is not fully fair or diagnostic. Most baselines are all-atom 3D generators without access to the same reaction grammar, while the retrained SEMLAFLOW baseline appears weaker than expected and does not isolate which parts of SYNCOGEN’s advantage come from hard constraints versus learned modeling.

The chemical realism of the synthetic routes is weakly validated. The paper explicitly ignores protecting groups, stoichiometry, directing effects, and other practical issues, yet repeatedly claims streamlined practical synthesis; there is no experimental validation or expert assessment of route feasibility.

The inpainting/fragment-linking evaluation is much too limited for the strength of the drug-discovery claims: only three targets, mostly docking/AF3-style proxy evaluation, low valid rates for SYNCOGEN, and a comparison to DiffLinker under different constraints and objectives.

Several evaluation details reduce confidence: retrosynthesis is evaluated on only 100 samples in places, uncertainty/error bars are mostly absent, FCD and distributional comparisons are difficult to interpret across different training distributions, and Table 5 actually shows SYNCOGEN worse than RDKit on both COV and MAT despite being described as similar quality.

The method relies on several heuristic constraints and sampling choices, including compatibility masking, parent pruning, inference annealing, and non-equivariant coordinate handling. These may be reasonable engineering choices, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze their failure modes or theoretical implications.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the dataset and code links appear blank, and important choices such as exact data splits, baseline training parity, and route evaluation settings are not documented enough to support the strongest claims.

The novelty is incremental relative to existing masked diffusion/flow models and synthesis-aware generation work: the combination is interesting, but the contribution appears more like a specialized engineering integration than a broadly validated new generative modeling advance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: jointly generating synthesizable molecules and 3D coordinates, rather than treating synthetic accessibility and geometry as separate post-hoc concerns.

The proposed representation over building blocks, reaction templates, reaction centers, and coordinates is well motivated, and the joint masked discrete diffusion plus coordinate flow formulation is technically interesting.

The SYNSPACE dataset is a valuable contribution: it is synthesis-aware, includes reaction-graph structure, and provides millions of low-energy conformers, enabling a class of models that existing 2D synthesis datasets or 3D conformer datasets do not support well.

The empirical results are broadly convincing. SYNCOGEN substantially improves validity, retrosynthesis solve rates, and several geometry/energy metrics relative to strong 3D molecular generation baselines, while also returning synthetic routes.

The paper includes useful ablations showing that chemistry-aware constraints, self-conditioning, and other training/sampling choices matter. The fragment-linking/inpainting demonstration is a compelling proof of concept for downstream drug-design use cases.
The method and limitations are described with unusual chemical specificity, including reaction-center injectivity, building-block construction, conformer generation, and known simplifications.
weaknesses: The comparison set is somewhat imperfect for the main claim. Most baselines are unconstrained atom-level 3D generators rather than synthesis-aware 3D generators, so the results partly compare different problem settings. The paper would be stronger with more direct comparisons to synthesis-aware methods, even if only in 2D plus conformer-generation pipelines.

The generated chemical space is narrow: only 93 building blocks, 19 reaction templates, 2-4 sequential reactions, no macrocycles, simplified boron chemistry, and no protection/stoichiometry/directing-group handling. This supports reliable synthesis-like generation, but limits the generality of the claimed synthesizability advantage.

Reproducibility is weakened by apparent placeholder links for dataset/code availability in the extracted manuscript. For a dataset-and-model paper, public release details, licenses, preprocessing scripts, and exact baseline checkpoints are important.

The synthesizability evaluation is limited: retrosynthesis solve rates are computed on only 100 generated examples, and the template grammar itself bakes in much of the synthesizability. Experimental validation or at least larger-scale route verification would better support the practical claims.

Some headline claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, the paper claims state-of-the-art 3D molecule generation, but appendix distribution metrics show SYNCOGEN is not uniformly best on bond lengths, angles, dihedrals, or energy distances, and conformer generation with a fixed graph is slightly worse than RDKit ETKDG in Table 5.

The molecular inpainting evaluation is promising but small and somewhat anecdotal: only three targets, no retraining, reliance on docking and AlphaFold3 predictions, and substantially lower validity than DiffLinker. It demonstrates potential, but not yet robust practical performance.
The coordinate noising scheme explicitly breaks equivariance under some masking conditions. The paper acknowledges this, but the impact is not deeply analyzed beyond aggregate performance.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: synthesizable 3D molecular generation with explicit reaction routes, rather than treating synthesizability only as a post-hoc score.

The joint formulation over building-block reaction graphs and coordinates is conceptually strong and well matched to the problem. Combining masked discrete diffusion for reaction graphs with flow matching for coordinates is a reasonable and useful modeling contribution.
The SYNSPACE dataset family is a valuable resource if released as claimed, with sizable coverage, conformers, pharmacophore annotations, and explicit building block/reaction provenance.

Empirical coverage is broad: unconditional generation, fragment-linking/inpainting, pharmacophore-conditioned generation, larger-vocabulary experiments, training and sampling ablations, and comparisons to multiple recent 3D molecular generators.

Results show clear advantages on synthesizability-related metrics and strong validity, while maintaining reasonable coordinate quality and diversity. The ablations support the importance of chemistry-aware constraints and self-conditioning.
weaknesses: The strongest claims of state-of-the-art 3D generation are somewhat overstated. In the appendix, SYNCOGEN is not consistently best on geometry distribution metrics, energy distribution distances, or graph-conditioned conformer generation, and Table 7 shows it underperforming RDKit ETKDG on coverage and matching accuracy.

The baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. Some baselines are not synthesis-aware by design, and not all appear to be retrained on SYNSPACE; therefore gains in synthesizability and FCD partly reflect the constrained generation space and dataset construction rather than purely superior modeling.

The synthesizability guarantee is weaker than the framing suggests. The reaction grammar is simplified, omits protection/selectivity/stoichiometry/directing effects, collapses stereochemical issues, and does not experimentally validate yield or feasibility. Retrosynthesis solve rates are also computed on only 100 samples for some evaluations.

Conditional drug-discovery experiments rely heavily on docking, PoseBusters, and selected AlphaFold3 examples, all of which are proxy evaluations. The fragment-linking task uses only three targets, and the pharmacophore task uses ten targets, so the evidence for broad drug-discovery impact is promising but not definitive.

The design space is relatively narrow: the main model uses 93 building blocks and 19 templates, with 2-4 reactions. This is practical and controlled, but limits claims about general de novo molecular design; the larger-vocabulary result shows some degradation in validity/PoseBusters.

Reproducibility is claimed, but the manuscript text contains blank code/data links in the introduction. For a dataset- and system-heavy paper, actual availability of code, checkpoints, reactions, building blocks, and generation scripts is central.

The paper would benefit from a clearer comparison to concurrent CGFlow and other synthesis-pathway methods, especially separating what is due to amortized conditioning, what is due to reaction-graph representation, and what is due to the curated search space.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical gap: connecting 3D molecular generation with explicit synthesis-aware reaction graphs, which is a relevant and potentially useful direction for molecular design.
The proposed SYNSPACE dataset family is a useful engineering contribution in principle, pairing building-block reaction graphs with generated conformers and pharmacophore annotations.

The model integrates discrete masked diffusion for reaction graphs with continuous coordinate flow matching in a coherent framework, and the paper includes several ablations on constraints, self-conditioning, schedules, and vocabulary size.
The experiments cover multiple settings, including unconditional generation, fragment linking, and pharmacophore-conditioned generation, rather than only a single benchmark.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are much stronger than the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims state-of-the-art performance and practical drug-discovery relevance, but the evaluations are mostly in silico, use generated/procedural datasets, and rely heavily on docking, retrosynthesis solvers, and force-field proxies.

The comparison to baselines is not fully fair or well controlled. Many baselines are atom-level 3D generators not designed to enforce reaction-template synthesizability, so higher retrosynthesis scores are partly built into the restricted search space rather than demonstrating a superior generative model. Conversely, synthesis-aware 2D methods and 3D methods are compared under different conditioning assumptions.

The synthesizability claim is under-supported. Molecules are generated from a limited reaction/building-block grammar, but the paper does not convincingly validate reaction feasibility, selectivity, yields, stereochemistry, protecting-group issues, or multi-step route practicality. Retrosynthesis solve rates are computed on only 100 samples and do not substitute for validating the proposed forward routes.

The dataset is procedurally generated from small curated vocabularies, which raises concerns about diversity, bias, and leakage between train/test-style evaluations. Novelty and FCD against this synthetic training distribution are not enough to establish broad molecular design utility.

The conditional drug-discovery experiments are weak. Fragment-linking uses only three hand-selected targets whose ligands contain compatible building blocks, and pharmacophore generation is evaluated with best/median docking over 100 samples per target. Docking and AlphaFold-style qualitative overlays are insufficient evidence for binding or lead quality.

Several results undermine the strongest claims. Appendix distributional metrics show SYNCOGEN is not consistently best on bond lengths, angles, dihedrals, or energy distribution distances, and zero-shot conformer generation is worse than RDKit ETKDG on the reported COV/MAT metrics.

The method appears to rely heavily on hard chemistry constraints and restricted generation rather than a clearly novel modeling advance. The architecture is adapted from existing SE(3)-equivariant flow models, with discrete diffusion and compatibility masking layered on top; the paper does not isolate the novelty strongly enough.

Reproducibility is concerning: the main text contains blank code/data links, and many critical implementation details are deferred to appendices. Given the complexity of the chemistry pipeline, reaction templates, conformer generation, and evaluation stack, missing accessible artifacts would be a major issue.

The paper does not sufficiently discuss limitations from the restricted reaction set, absence of experimental validation, stereochemical collapse, and potential failure modes in generated synthetic routes. The ethics statement is also quite shallow for a dual-use molecular generation system.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: combining 3D molecular generation with explicit synthesis-aware reaction/building-block structure. This is a meaningful gap in current molecular generative modeling.
weaknesses: The central performance claims are somewhat overstated. SYNCOGEN is not uniformly state-of-the-art on conformer quality metrics; appendix results show several atom-based baselines outperform it on bond length/angle/dihedral or energy distribution distances, even if they lack synthesis routes.
